extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, induction, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and producing reliable scientific observations, descriptions, and hypotheses—distinguishing perception from inference and explaining when inductive generalizations are warranted. Useful for those learning or applying inductive logic in empirical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of a scientific hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming a hypothesis is a legitimate scientific act even when founded on slight grounds, provided it is tentative and useful to guide inquiry; hypotheses need not claim proof but must be admissible and discussable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Gilbert's hypothesis that the earth is a magnet; suggestions that the brain is a voltaic pile; Gall's localisation attempts. A hypothesis may be valuable by opening a promising path of inquiry even if verification is difficult. Verification requires observation and experiment; hypotheses should be judged by their capacity to be rendered discussable and amenable to inquiry rather than by immediate conformity to inductive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rules of Hypothesis from rules of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are governed by the rules appropriate to hypothesizing (framing plausible conjectures), whereas Induction concerns conditions of proof; one is not bound to the rigorous proof-conditions of Induction when proposing a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's discussion of Darwin: Darwin did not pretend his doctrine was proved and thus was not violating rules of Induction; he was acting within rules of Hypothesis. Evaluate whether a proposed idea fulfills the procedural criteria for a legitimate hypothesis (e.g., plausibility, discussability), separately from whether it satisfies inductive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation must be actual perception, not inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole condition for relying on an observation is that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; it must be an observation, not an inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'I hear a man's voice'—the direct perception is hearing a sound; that it is 'a man's voice' is an inference. When assessing observational claims, ask whether the claim asserts raw sensation or further inferred facts. Only the former constitutes pure observation for logical reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate perception from inference in reports
rubrics_metrics.description: In any act of perceiving and in its description, observation and inference are often blended; the logic of observation requires correct discrimination between sensations (perceptions) and the inferences drawn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: when recording or evaluating an observation, remove inferred elements and retain only the sensations or states of consciousness as the observational datum. Whatever remains as inference should be treated under the rules of induction rather than as immediate evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of sense are errors of judgement (inference) not of sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent errors of the senses (optical illusions, mistaken identifications) are in fact erroneous inferences from genuine sensations; the sensations themselves are genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: kaleidoscope, seeing a candle through a multiplying glass, mistaking a person at a distance, hallucinations or dreams. Anti-pattern: blaming the senses rather than inspecting the inferential step from sensation to object-identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive generalizations can be more reliable than single instances
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from many particular instances may deserve more complete reliance than any single particular statement, because individual particulars often involve inferential error that is unlikely to be repeated across many independent instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement: number of instances must be sufficient to eliminate chance. Use repeated, independent observations as an index to the stability and intensity of the underlying cause; beware changes in the collocation of causes that would invalidate extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description inherently involves classification and resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe an observed fact is necessarily to assert a resemblance between that fact and other things; description therefore always introduces elements beyond the bare sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: saying 'I see something white' not only reports a sensation but classifies it by resemblance to the category 'white.' Recognize that any descriptive statement contains conceptual additions (classificatory claims) that must be evaluated and cannot be treated as raw perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic's role: assess when observation may be relied on (not how to train observers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic concerns the conditions under which observation is trustworthy for purposes of evidence and induction; it does not prescribe educational methods for making better observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the logical evaluation of observational evidence (is this truly an observation vs inference?) from pedagogical concerns (how to teach someone to observe better). For logical analysis, focus on reliability conditions and discrimination of senses vs inferences.
